data.title: Wall Street ends down, calls for AI slowdown pummel chipmakers
data.description:
Key points:
  • Chipmakers drop after call for slower AI development
  • 10-year yield climbs above 5%
  • S&P 500 PE dips to its lowest since April 2025

By Noel Randewich

Wall Street ended down on Monday, weighed down by losses in Nvidia and other chipmakers after top executives in U.S. artificial intelligence companies raised safety concerns and called for a slowdown in the development of AI.

Investors were also jittery after the benchmark 10-year Treasury yield briefly surpassed 5% for the first time since 2023 ahead of this week's Federal Reserve meeting. The U.S. central bank is widely expected to raise interest rates.

AI-linked stocks plunged worldwide after the leaders of Anthropic, OpenAI and xAI warned of risks from rapid development, the starkest threat yet to the billions of dollars being poured into the industry that have driven markets to record highs.

Shares of Nvidia , Broadcom , Micron Technology and Advanced Micro Devices declined, and the PHLX chip index fell sharply.

Brent crude futures settled 1% higher at $105.68 per barrel as worries about energy supplies mounted following new strikes on Saudi Arabian energy infrastructure and attacks on ships in the Middle East.

High inflation, heavy corporate and government borrowing and concerns about the long-term U.S. fiscal trajectory have sent U.S. Treasury yields higher in the past month. The 5% mark that the 10-year yield hit on Monday is a threshold that analysts warned could ripple through the U.S. economy and threaten the bull market in stocks by denting the relative appeal of U.S. equities.

Traders are pricing in a 90% chance that the Fed will raise interest rates by 25 basis points at its policy meeting on Wednesday to fight inflation related to high oil prices, according to CME's FedWatch.

"The 10-year going above 5% is huge and speaks volumes, and it may pressure the Fed to do more than just one rate hike," said Jake Dollarhide, CEO of Longbow Asset Management.

According to preliminary data, the S&P 500 lost 36.93 points, or 0.48%, to end at 7,620.05 points, while the Nasdaq Composite lost 145.25 points, or 0.55%, to 26,187.79. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 151.66 points, or 0.29%, to 52,421.63.

ServiceNow , Adobe and Workday rallied. Those and other software stocks have sold off in recent sessions over worries that competition from AI companies could hurt their margins.

Bank of America dipped after CEO Brian Moynihan said he expects investment banking fees to drop by at least 10% in the third quarter.

The S&P 500's recent decline, coupled with a strong earnings outlook, has the benchmark trading at 19 times expected earnings. That is its cheapest since April 2025, when U.S. President Donald Trump's "Liberation Day" tariff announcements threw global markets into a tailspin.

data.title: Mirum Pharmaceuticals Reports Inducement Grants Under Nasdaq Listing Rule 5635(c)(4)
data.description:
Mirum Pharmaceuticals, Inc. (Nasdaq: MIRM), a leading rare disease company, today announced that on September 10, 2026, the Compensation Committee of Mirum’s Board of Directors granted inducement awards consisting of non-qualified stock options to purchase 28,512 shares of common stock and 37,375 restricted stock units (“RSUs”) to 14 new employees under Mirum’s 2020 Inducement Plan. The Compensation Committee of Mirum’s Board of Directors approved the awards as an inducement material to the new employees’ employment in accordance with Nasdaq Listing Rule 5635(c)(4).

Each stock option has an exercise price of $100.61 per share, which is equal to the closing price of Mirum’s common stock on September 10, 2026, and will vest over four years, with 25% of the underlying shares vesting on the one-year anniversary of the applicable vesting commencement date, and the balance of the underlying shares vesting monthly thereafter over 36 months, subject to the new employees’ continued service relationship with Mirum through the applicable vesting dates. The RSUs will vest over three years, with 33% of the underlying shares vesting on each anniversary of the applicable initial vesting date, subject to the new employees’ continued service relationship with Mirum through the applicable vesting dates. The awards are subject to the terms and conditions of Mirum’s 2020 Inducement Plan and the terms and conditions of an applicable award agreement covering the grant.

About Mirum Pharmaceuticals

Mirum Pharmaceuticals (NASDAQ: MIRM) is a leading rare disease company with a global footprint of approved products and a broad pipeline of investigational medicines. Purpose-built to bring forward breakthrough medicines for people with overlooked conditions, Mirum focuses on rare liver and rare genetic diseases, where it has built deep expertise and strong connections to patient communities. The company’s commercial portfolio includes LIVMARLI® (maralixibat) for Alagille syndrome (ALGS) and progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis (PFIC), CHOLBAM® (cholic acid) for bile-acid synthesis disorders, and CTEXLI® (chenodiol) for cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis (CTX).

Mirum’s clinical-stage pipeline includes volixibat, an IBAT inhibitor in late-stage development for primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) and primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), brelovitug, a fully human monoclonal antibody in late-stage development for chronic hepatitis delta virus (HDV), zilurgisertib, an ALK2 inhibitor under regulatory review with the FDA for fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP), and MRM-3379, a PDE4D inhibitor being evaluated for Fragile X syndrome (FXS).

Mirum’s success is driven by a team dedicated to advancing high impact medicines through strategic development, disciplined execution and purposeful collaboration across the rare disease ecosystem. Learn more at www.mirumpharma.com and follow Mirum on Facebook, LinkedIn, Instagram and X.

data.title: Law firm Morgan & Morgan touts $1 billion AI investment, plans to sell platform to other firms
data.description:
By Sara Merken

Morgan & Morgan, which bills itself as the largest U.S. personal injury law firm, said on Monday that it has committed to investing at least $1 billion into AI and technology over the next decade and will begin marketing its own AI platform to other law firms next year.

The Orlando, Florida-based firm said it already spent $300 million building its AI platform, called MX2, which it said it uses to extract medical information, generate case documents and prepare for trials. It said the platform now has nearly 5,000 monthly users.

The investment will include hiring personnel and building new software and security capabilities, Yath Ithayakumar, the firm's chief transformation officer, said in an interview. The majority "is going to be very targeted towards AI," he said.

The announcement comes as major corporate defense law firms are also investing heavily in AI. Kirkland & Ellis said in May that it is devoting $500 million of its revenue to developing a custom AI platform over the next three to four years.

Other law firms have inked agreements with major technology companies to jointly create AI tools. London-based Freshfields said in April it will work with the legal team at Anthropic, the maker of Claude, to develop AI applications for legal services. Reuters' parent company Thomson Reuters also sells AI-assisted tools for ​the legal industry.

Morgan & Morgan founder John Morgan said in a statement that his firm, with more than 1,100 lawyers, was ahead of its rivals in AI adoption and that trial-focused firms like his were more insulated than corporate firms from being replaced by the technology.

"Firms which bill by the hour to draft and review agreements or read through thousands of pages of documents are the practices AI will replace – almost entirely," he said.

The firm said it plans to make MX2 available to other law firms, including corporate and transactional practices, by the end of 2027 on an invitation-only basis.

"We think we're in a great position to help law firms solve tough problems and we're confident we can do it," Ithayakumar said. The firm did not say how it would price access to the platform.

Reuters had reported in June that Morgan & Morgan, which has annual revenue of $2.4 billion, had hired JPMorgan to explore a minority stake sale that could eventually make way for the firm to go public.

Widespread AI adoption by lawyers is expected to speed their work, but it has also created problems when attorneys have relied on AI-generated results without checking their accuracy. A federal judge in Wyoming sanctioned two lawyers from Morgan & Morgan last year for citing fake cases generated by AI in a court filing.

Ithayakumar said the error in the case took place "because we were early adopters of AI and we were moving fast." He said the firm has invested in training processes to make it easier for lawyers and staff to review AI outputs.

data.title: U.S. 10-Year Yield Cools After Topping 5%; German Bund Yield Hits 15-Year High — Update
data.description:
By Emese Bartha and Paulo Trevisani

U.S. Treasury yields lost steam after reaching multi-year highs on Monday as investors grapple with the prospect of rising borrowing costs amid volatility in energy markets.

The 10-year Treasury yield rose past 5% for the first time since October 2023, before stabilizing slightly lower. The move mirrored oil prices, which rallied nearly 5% in early trade before easing to a 1% gain Monday afternoon. The dollar followed, strengthening in the morning against major currencies, then cooling later in the day.

The 10-year German Bund yield hit another 15-year high of 3.538%.

Investors are worried that central banks can no longer ignore higher prices, and will eventually have to raise interest rates.

"The spike in energy prices...has caught everyone's attention, including, in our view, the attention of the central banks," Neuberger portfolio manager Joseph Purtell said. Monetary policymakers "now are in a position where they are no longer just looking through these energy price shocks," he said.

That prospect will be tested Wednesday when the Federal Reserve is widely expected to raise rates for the first time since 2023, potentially launching a cycle of rising interest rates. Chairman Kevin Warsh will be pressured to provide some clarity, despite his aversion to forward guidance

"A cautious message on inflation fighting could deepen the credibility discount on U.S. bonds," said Paolo Zanghieri, senior economist at Generali Investments. "A forceful inflation warning could fuel expectations of a hiking cycle and push short-end yields higher."

U.S. money markets priced a 93% probability that the Fed will hike rates by a quarter of a percent, according to LSEG.

"The repricing [in U.S. interest-rate expectations] has kept Treasury yields elevated and provided support to the greenback," said Wael Makarem, a financial markets strategist at Exness. "Beyond this week, markets are pricing in further tightening this year and the next."

Across the Atlantic, elevated oil prices continue to pose an inflationary threat for Europe, with Brent crude at $106 a barrel.

The European Central Bank raised interest rates last week, bringing the deposit rate to 2.50%--a level widely viewed as the upper bound of neutral policy. The central bank also revised up its inflation forecasts for 2027 and 2028, alongside higher GDP projections for 2026 and 2027.

Some forecasters still see an argument for another Fed hold, given the volatility of energy prices.

Simon Ballard, chief economist at First Abu Dhabi Bank, said in a note that "monetary policy is a relatively blunt tool for combating geopolitically fuelled inflation." He expects the Fed to "keep its powder dry this week and allow the macro data backdrop to evolve before risking a more restrictive monetary policy stance."

Write to Emese Bartha at emese.bartha@wsj.com and to Paulo Trevisani at paulo.trevisani@wsj.com.

data.title: Treasury Yields Slip After Hitting Multi-Year Highs — Market Talk
data.description:
1552 ET - Treasury yields give back early increases and settle just below Friday levels, as investors grapple with volatile oil prices and their potential impact on the global economy. Crude futures rise 1%, cooling from a pace as fast as 5% in early trade. A dollar rally also slows during the day. Markets now price 93% odds of a Fed hike Wednesday, according to LSEG. The 10-year yield drops 0.014 percentage point to 4.960%, after rising above 5% in the morning for the first time since 2023. The two-year declines 0.010 point to 4.632%, after hitting its highest level since 2024. Both snap a five-day rising streak. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

1510 ET - Roblox used its annual developers conference to highlight expansion of its catalog to browser and App Store-based games, an offline playing option, and an AI game development tool for non-technical creators, Wedbush says in a note. The company needs to retain developers and show investors a path back toward accelerating growth, and its updates at the conference were a start, the analysts say. "Roblox has a substantial opportunity ahead and is laying the groundwork well," they write. "We need more evidence on the monetization side, and specifically on the timeline for these initiatives to show up in bookings, before turning more constructive." They keep a perform rating but raise their price target to $48 from $40. Wells Fargo and Bank of America also lift their price targets on the stock. Shares gain 11%.(elias.schisgall@wsj.com)

1415 ET - Royal Bank of Canada chief economist Frances Donald and her team say they are cautiously optimistic about the Canadian outlook despite uncertainty swirling about US-Canada trade. She forecasts sub-2% growth this year and next but argues the economy is stronger on a per-capita basis amid stalled population growth. The commodity-rich provinces in western Canada are leading the charge on growth. RBC expects four Bank of Canada rate hikes next year, taking the policy rate to 3.25%, due to concern over higher energy prices and an improving economy. Still, Donald adds "there are growing risks that [the] first hike could come" later in 2026. (Paul.Vieira@wsj.com; @paulvieira)

1231 ET - Treasury yields decline from multi-year highs, but elevated borrowing costs could be a new normal as a combination of drivers undermine demand for government debt. "I think a major factor is, basically, a big demand for capital from the AI buildout," Societe Generale's Jan Groen says. "And on top of that, we have a lot of demand from the federal government [and] a lot of uncertainty about the Fed, whether they actually will start hiking." Groen expects the Fed to start hiking this week and repeat every other meeting through March. Fiscal worries, however, are here to stay. "There is a real risk that fiscal dominance will be an issue for monetary policy going forward," he says. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

1230 ET - Underlying price pressures in Canada remain contained, and the share of categories in the consumer-price index continue to be benign, Nomura's Ruchir Sharma says. The economist says that despite higher input costs the pass through to consumer prices has been limited. Shelter inflation picked up modestly in August but remained below 2%, and recent data suggests market rents continue to decline, and goods inflation remains soft while food inflation continues to cool. "Overall, the August report suggests inflation remains subdued and close to the Bank of Canada's target," says Sharma, who continues to expect interest rates to remain on hold through 2026. (robb.stewart@wsj.com; @RobbMStewart)

1218 ET - National Bank of Canada economist Mathieu Arseneau says it would be "premature" for the Bank of Canada to raise rates in October, even though headline inflation remains elevated and fears intensify over a prolonged Mideast conflict. Arseneau says core CPI remains "generally contained" near 2%, wage gains have sharply decelerated and US trade policy remains a stiff headwind. He adds the inflation data still suggests the energy shock is not, at this time, spilling over broadly into the CPI basket of goods. (paul.vieira@wsj.com; @paulvieira)

1215 ET - Scotiabank's Derek Holt reckons the latest data strongly suggests the Bank of Canada is behind the curve in fighting inflation. The consumer-price index dipped 0.1% on-month in August and was steady at 3% annually. However, Holt says traditional core CPI excluding food and energy landed at 3.9% on-month seasonally adjusted, annualized, which is the hottest since April 2025. The three-moving average is 3.6% on the same basis, and the four-month average is 3.6%, he adds. Core inflation is on a tear in Canada and that continues to support an interest rate increase at the Bank of Canada's October meeting, Holt argues. (robb.stewart@wsj.com; @RobbMStewart)

1157 ET - The yield on Canada's two-year government bond trades at 3.41%, or the highest level in over two years — or July 31, 2024. Back in July of 2024, the Bank of Canada's policy rate was at 4.50%, on a downward trend after taming historically high inflation. The two-year yield is now 50 basis points higher from a low reached in late August, and this reflects growing concern over inflation and the need for higher interest rates. Some economists note the BOC doesn't necessarily need to raise rates given the gap between the policy rate, at 2.25%, and the 2-year yield, because the selloff in the bond market is de facto tightening monetary conditions. (paul.vieira@wsj.com)

1123 ET - August's retail sales, due Wednesday, should see a rebound from a sharp drop in July, according to an analysis from BofA. A positive reading paired with August's better-than-expected jobs report should reassure investors the economy was stronger than July's jobs report and retail sales suggested. The slide in July retail sales was due to Prime Day and related promotions shifting to June from July this year, BofA says. In August, total BAC card spending per household was up 4.5% year-over-year, according to the economists. Overall, August retail sales are expected to climb 0.8% according to WSJ consensus versus a 0.6% decline in July.(jessica.coacci@wsj.com)

1117 ET - Investors have sharply raised their expectations of Bank of England interest-rate increases over the coming months after Brent crude advanced above $109 a barrel. Markets see a 47% probability of a BOE rate rise at Thursday's policy decision, and fully price in two rate rises by year-end, LSEG data show. Traders are fully pricing in four BOE rate increases by April 2027, a notable increase from the two priced in a week ago, according to LSEG data. As a result, U.K. 2-year gilt yields have surged to 4.979%, their highest since 2023, the LSEG data show. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

1057 ET - New home construction is starting to slow, Zillow says. Completion of detached single-family homes fell for the third straight year in 2025, and the pace of permitting is slipping further below its pre-pandemic trend line. The concern is that a thinner pipeline could deepen an already significant housing shortage at a time when affordability is already stretched thin. Over the 12 months ending July 2026, more than 1.42 million residential building permits were issued nationwide, down 1.7% from the same period a year earlier. Compared with the pre-pandemic trajectory from 2016 through 2020, permitting is running 19.4% below where it would have been if that trend had held. Permitting has fallen year over year for 44 consecutive months. (chris.wack@wsj.com)

1052 ET - The dollar strengthens as U.S. interest rates keep rising. "The combination of heightened expectations for the Federal Reserve to lift rates late this week coupled with the high oil prices have helped lift the U.S. dollar broadly today," Bannockburn's Marc Chandler writes. The WSJ Dollar Index is up 0.5%, as the greenback strengthens 0.8% against the yen and 0.6% versus the euro. Inflation expectations are rising, as measured by the derivatives market, while Treasury yields reach multi-year highs and the 10-year benchmark surpasses 5%. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

data.title: Why Google and Meta Stocks Are the Big Winners From the Latest AI Concerns — Barrons.com
data.description:
By George Glover

Google owner Alphabet and Facebook parent Meta Platforms have been frustrating stocks to own in 2026-but they were getting some love from investors on Monday, even as a broader tech selloff raged on.

Alphabet climbed 1.8% and Meta added 1.4% in early trading. The Nasdaq 100 fell 1.7% after the bosses of Anthropic, OpenAI, and SpaceX called for a slowdown in AI development.

The two Big Tech companies could benefit from a co-ordinated slowdown by the developers of Claude, ChatGPT, and Grok. Both Meta and Google are working on rival AI systems.

Google released the latest version of its Gemini chatbot, Gemini 3.8 Flash, earlier this month, while Meta's consumer AI agent Muse hit the App Store's top three last week.

But the latest iterations of Gemini and Muse both rank behind Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.1, OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra, and SpaceX's Grok-4.6, according to OpenLM's large-language model leaderboard.

If the three biggest AI companies slow down development, that could level the playing field.

The concerns about AI risks should also give both companies room to reposition, with Meta focused on data-center rental and Google leaning into its distribution and chip businesses, New Street Research analyst Dan Salmon said.

Shares of Alphabet and Meta have struggled for direction in 2026 as investors pile into chip and memory stocks. Alphabet was up 8.2% for the year through Friday's close, while Meta was down 1.8%.

Write to George Glover at george.glover@dowjones.com

data.title: Serbia's President Vucic says he will run for prime minister amid student protests
data.description:
Serbia's President Aleksandar Vucic, a populist who has been ‌president or prime minister for 12 years, said he would run for prime minister in an October 25 election, and thousands of opposition supporters rallied in Belgrade on Monday.

Vucic has faced nearly two years of student-led anti-corruption demonstrations triggered by a railway station roof collapse that killed 16 people in the city of Novi Sad in November 2024.

On Monday evening, thousands gathered in central Belgrade to support parliamentary candidates for the "Students Win" movement, the main opposition. The candidates submitted certified signatures of their supporters, the initial step to get on the ballot.

Vucic, who said in June he would resign but did not give a date, called the snap election for October 25.

"I would like to inform you that on September 27 I will resign as president," Vucic told Pink TV on Sunday evening. "That evening I will address the nation and thank people for their support."

Some opposition parties including the Democratic Party and Kreni Promeni Movement have pledged their support to the student movement and will not field candidates.

At the rally, students carried Serbian flags and shouted "Students Win."

"We, as students, want to reset the system and start everything from the beginning, so that institutions can do their jobs," said student Stefan Lukic, who attended the event.

Students and opposition parties accuse Vucic and his allies of corruption and controlling the media, which they deny.

data.title: AirBaltic in talks with unions to cut workers amid restructuring, CEO says
data.description:
By Joanna Plucinska

AirBaltic is in talks with labour unions to come to an agreement on an "adjustment in the workforce," Chief Executive Erno Hilden told Reuters on Monday after the Latvian carrier announced it was voluntarily entering Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings.

"We are currently carrying out the consultations with the labour unions," Hilden said, adding that with plans to reduce capacity, a change in workforce is a "natural conclusion."

"When all of that is concluded, then it is going to be time to really come up with numbers."

AirBaltic filed for protection under Chapter 11 of the U.S. Bankruptcy Code in New York on Monday as it seeks to restructure its debt pile, head off creditors and survive a deepening sector-wide crisis brought on by the Iran war.

Hilden, previously CFO for Scandinavian Airlines where he steered the firm through a similar bankruptcy process, added that there would be no interruption or change expected to airBaltic's operations during the Chapter 11 proceedings.

He added the biggest changes would involve the carrier's so-called "wet lease" business, where it loans out its planes and crew to other carriers for a fee.

The chairperson of the Latvian aviation union, Dace Kavasa, told Reuters talks were taking place about instituting "alternative employment solutions", including allowing some workers to stay on part-time and it was still unclear how many people would be dismissed.

"The collective dismissal consultations are ongoing. There are a lot of unknowns. There are still quite serious disagreements on the objectivity of some proposed criteria," Kavasa said, adding that they were hoping for some constructive decisions by the end of the week.
